messages.body_plain:
Hi Kylie,

it appears that when I was reading in the raw data with the resolution specified in ppm, then the lower mz values appear rounded as compared to the higher ones, which end up with a lot of decimals for some reason (in my understanding the m/z resolution should be lower for the higher m/zs). I am not sure why, but when I read in with resolution specified in m/z, then everything is as it should be.

The reason why I played with the resolution so much is that my peak maps have been looking very bad, not very smooth, with individual pixels appearing as holes in the maps (in comparison, the MSiReader maps I get with the default settings are beautiful, so it does not have to do with the raw data). To me it looks like the respective peak was not detected in the hole-pixels, it could be that the centroid algorighm in MSiReader works better for my data, but also just that some of the parameters I set in Cardinal are not good choices for my data. I have tried out so many combinations by now, various resolutions, lowering the SNR threshold, increasing the tolerance for peak alignment and trying out the new peakbin method. Nothing helped, so I feel like I missed something fundamental, and at the moment my approach is really just trial&error, so I was wondering whether there is a way to make some educated guesses on how to determine the best parameters for the whole processing pipeline. My main doubts are still with regard to the resolution. Do you have any indications for what is a reasonable resolution to read in data (with respect to the resolving power of the machine) and whether it is better read in the data with very high resolution and then Gaussian-smooth it, rather than binning it during read-in?

And do you have any recommendations for what should the peakpick / peakbin tolerance be in relation to the resolution? Am I right to think that I read in my data e.g. in the resolution of 0.002, then doing peak align with a tolerance of <= 0.002 will not really do anything, because any bins other than the one of my peak are already outside the tolerance? So if at the end of the day I want to be able to distinguish peaks with an m/z accuracy of 0.002, I'd need to read in my data with a higher resolution?

I'd be very grateful for any pointers!!
Thanks, Ilona

messages.subject: Re: Peak align fails
messages.body_plain:
I am not sure how to interpret the m/z values appearing rounded, as there should be no rounding if you're working with MSImagingExperiment. R may print fewer significant digits for some numbers than others, which may look like rounding. The bins start at the next-lowest-integer relative to the first observed m/z-value in the dataset, so the first few m/z-values may appear "neater" than the last, after many many small numbers have been accumulated. This is likely just an issue with the number of decimal places R chooses to print.

It is difficult to determine the best pre-processing parameters for data unseen or in a general case, which is why they are available for the user to adjust.

However, you're correct that if you want to distinguish peaks with an accuracy of m/z 0.002, then the data should be binned with a much higher resolution than 0.002; otherwise, you're not getting any peak shape, which is typically necessary for the peak picking to work properly. Attempting align peaks with the same tolerance as was originally used to bin the data doesn't really accomplish anything that couldn't be accomplished more simply by filtering the mass features, which may be what you should be doing instead.

The "holes" you're seeing are likely indeed spectra where that peak was not detected. This is typically going to happen when peak-picking on individual spectra and aligning the peaks. That's the purpose of peakBin(): to sweep back through the dataset and bin peaks using a list of reference m/z values. However, for peak binning to work also requires the peak shape, because the algorithm attempts to look for the peak center and then expand it to the local minima. If you're expecting the find peaks 0.002 m/z apart but you're data is already binned to 0.002 m/z resolution, then this will likely not work out, which may also be the source of your "holes". In this situation, you may need to use mzBin() with the reference m/z's of the peaks; mzBin() does not use the peak shape, and instead just bins to some fixed bin width.

If you want to extract peaks that are 0.002 apart but your data is already binned to 0.002, then you may try using mzFilter() with thresh.max=0.01 or something like that. This will just calculate the mean spectrum and then remove any m/z values with intensities less than some threshold proportion of the maximum mean intensity. This may produce the kind of dataset you want. (After doing this, you may want to set centroided(data) <- TRUE.)

I would suggest either:

1. Using either a higher bin resolution or a larger tolerance to do peak picking + binning.
2. If using .002 resolution, try using mzBin with the reference m/z's of the peaks instead of peakBin.
3. If using .002 resolution, try using mzFilter and skipping formal peak picking entirely

Hopefully one of these approaches may work for you.

messages.subject: Re: visualizing a ratio of two m/z images
messages.subject_clean: visualizing a ratio of two m/z images
messages.body_plain:
library(Cardinal)
data(pig206, package="CardinalWorkflows")
pig206 <- as(pig206, "MSImagingExperiment")

# plot some images
image(pig206, mz=888)
image(pig206, mz=563)

# get vectors of intensities
mz563 <- spectra(filter(pig206, mz=563))[1,]
mz888 <- spectra(filter(pig206, mz=888))[1,]
ratio <- (1 + mz888) / (1 + mz563)

# plot the ratio using formula interface
image(pig206, ratio ~ x * y, colorscale=divergent.colors)

# extract as arrays
i563 <- slice(pig206, mz=564)
i888 <- slice(pig206, mz=888)

image(i563 / i888)

Here is some code that does what you want. There are different ways of going about this.

Unfortunately, the image() method, while flexible, doesn't let you plot arithmetic combinations of different mass features.

So we need to extract the intensities first, calculate the ratio, and then use the formula argument to plot the result.

First, subset the data and extract the intensities as vectors. You could use bracketed indexing using [ instead of filter() to subset the data, but this requires knowing the row index of the associated m/z values, which we could find out with the features() function. Using filter() avoids that and produces an MSImagingExperiment with a single mass feature. Then use spectra() to extract the intensities as a matrix. I'm indexing here to get the intensities as a vector rather than a row-matrix.

I assign these vectors of intensities to variables and then calculate their ratio (I'm adding 1 to each to avoid creating Inf/NaN due to 0's).

Then I can use the formula argument of image() to plot the "ratio" variable I created.

Note that if your dataset is a regular rectangular grid, you can just set an appropriate dim() and you have your array.

Otherwise, we need to use slice(). This extracts an array from the dataset corresponding to some image. If the data is not on a regular grid, it may not reflect the underlying data exactly as some projections must be made. If the image is non-rectangular, then NAs will be introduced corresponding to the missing pixels.

-Kylie

So after digging around I've resolved the issue and thought I'd update in case anyone else runs into this.

The conversion process in my workflow generates an imzML file which contains x,y, and z coordinates (z=1) even though it is a 2D image. It seems the error was related to this z coordinate. Removing this (coord(data)$z<-NULL) resolved the issue.

I used msconvert to create a mzml file initially from Waters data, then imzMLConverter to create the imzML file.

Aalim

There is no error message or even a crash report from R? The whole computer? That's something...

The current release of spatialDGMM is a pure R implementation, so it is a bit slow, but shouldn't crash the system.

What are the dimensions of the dataset? (Number of pixels and number of features as given by dim()?)

Can you try subsetting the dataset to a smaller number of mass features and try SerialParam()?

It may be a parallelization issue. I expect BiocParallel to be stable, but sometimes it isn't, or sometimes there are socket connection issues.

-Kylie
